explanation: Cheraw is believed to have originated from a ritual performed to console the soul of a mother who died leaving a newborn child; it later became a festive/social performance, but its origin is classed as a ritual dance in most Mizo cultural references.
T.H. Lewin, a British official who wrote extensively on the Lushai, gave this etymology of "Mizo/Lushai" as 'head cutter' (lu = head, shai/sha = to cut).
The 1961 Census of India was the first to record Lushai, Hmar, Paihte, Pawi and Ralte sub-groups collectively self-identifying as 'Mizo'.

The Alexandrapore tea garden raid by Sailo chiefs Bengkhuaia and Savunga (in which Mary Winchester was abducted) took place in late January 1871; this was the trigger for the 1871-72 Lushai Expedition.
The First Lushai Expedition (a punitive British military expedition under Generals Bourchier and Brownlow, following the 1871 tea garden raids) was conducted in 1871-1872.
Under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971, the Mizo Hills district was carved out of Assam and declared the Union Territory of Mizoram on 21 January 1972.

In Mizo mythology the soul travels to Rih Dil, crosses Hringlang tlang for a last look at its village, then drinks water from Lunglohtui (the fountain of forgetfulness), and finally plucks the Hawilopar flower ('flower of no turning back') before moving on.

Mizo cultural sources record 'Khawzim pathian chuan mal min sawm leh ta a nih hi' ('Khawzim Pathian has delivered us from calamity') as part of the origin narrative told around the Pawl Kut harvest festival, tying the deity specifically to that kut rather than Mim Kut or Chapchar Kut.
Hmuichukchuriduninu, the bird-beaked child-eating witch of the forest, is the antagonist in the Mizo folktale of Nuchhimi, whose mother warns her to avoid the witch's path.

Sources consistently date the first missionary-run school in Mizoram (by Lorrain and Savidge) to 1 April 1894, which does not match any option here (1890-1893). This looks like a flawed/printing-error question; 1893 (the closest year, and also cited as when early government Hindi-medium schools began) is picked as the nearest plausible option.
The Mizo National Famine Front, formed by Laldenga to protest inadequate famine relief, dropped 'Famine' from its name and was formally converted into the Mizo National Front on 22 October 1961.

The mautam famine of 1861 (which destroyed the town of Tualte) is cited as the first major documented mautam-linked famine in the Lushai Hills among the years listed, predating the 1911 and later famines.
The provisional population total for Mizoram released as of 1 March 2011 was 1,091,014 (the final adjusted figure later published was 1,097,206).

Immediately after death, the Mizo believed the spirit's route to the afterlife began at Rih Dil (Rih Lake), the first waypoint on the journey, before it went on to Hringlang tlang and eventually Pialral or Mitthi khua.
Mizo (Lushai) is classified as a Kuki-Chin language within the larger Tibeto-Burman language family, not Indo-Aryan.
Khuallam ('dance of the guests'), performed during the Khuangchawi feast of merit, is also referred to as Thingdim lam in Mizo cultural references.
Fathang was the customary tribute of paddy (typically 1-3 baskets per household) paid annually by villagers to their chief in recognition of his authority over village land.
Under Mizo customary law, the party who lost a case before the chief's court paid a fine called 'Salam', usually valued at Rs. 5 or a pig.

'Dawvan' is documented as a raised platform attached to the zawlbuk that served as the meeting area for discussion, dispute settlement, and administrative business — functionally the closest match to a 'court-room' among the options — though sources describe it as part of the zawlbuk (bachelors' dormitory) complex rather than explicitly inside the chief's own house, so some uncertainty remains.
In the traditional Mizo calendar, Sahmulphah thla ('month to lay down fur', signalling the onset of winter) corresponds to November.

A Chemsen Bawi ('red knife slave') was a person who, having killed someone, sought the chief's protection/sanctuary; the chief was not owed labour but took paternal responsibility for the murderer's children.
Puanchei, the most prized and colourful of Mizo puans, is the special cloth a bride is required to bring and is customarily associated with entering the groom's house/wedding rites.

Lalthangfala Sailo received the Pu Buanga Award (the Mizo Academy of Letters' highest literary honour) in 2015, the most recent awardee before this 2016 exam; R.L. Thanmawia's award came later (around 2022), after this paper.
S.N. Barkataki, IAS, served as the last Superintendent and became the first Deputy Commissioner of the Lushai Hills district when the post was redesignated.
Hiteswar Saikia was the last Lieutenant Governor of Mizoram (1986-87) and, when Mizoram attained full statehood on 20 February 1987, became its first Governor.
Phawngpui (Blue Mountain), Mizoram's highest peak, stands at 2157 metres.
The Mizoram Liquor (Prohibition and Control) Act, 2014 was notified and came into force on 15 January 2015.

One government RTI-manual source dates the Taxation Department's bifurcation from the Excise & Taxation Department to July 1988, which does not match any of the four options given (2010/1973/2006/2009); this looks like a genuinely broken question. 2006 is kept only as an unverified placeholder within the given choices.
'Right now' signals an action in progress, requiring the present continuous tense 'is raining'.
Traditional Mizo wealth/status was measured by possessions such as Sial (mithun), Silai (guns) and Dar (brass gongs); 'Hmui' does not fit this set of recognised wealth-markers.

'Tangphel' appears listed among the traditional Mizo units of measurement (tehna) alongside hlam, ban chen and tawng chen used in house/land construction, which supports it being a length/spatial measure rather than a duration or body-size unit; its precise metric value could not be pinned down, so some uncertainty remains.
Hnawkhawl (Hnawkhal), a garment woven from tree bark/reed, is documented as the earliest form of clothing worn by Mizo men, distinct from the women's 'siapsuap'.
Thasiama Seno Neihna, a scenic plateau tied to a Mizo mithun-and-fairy legend, is located near Vaphai village in Champhai district.
Mitthirawp lam was a feast in which cotton effigies of ancestors were made, offered rice beer and meat, and paraded around the village to honour the spirits of the dead.
The Khawnglung Run (the massacre/raid on Khawnglung village, c. 1849-1856) is recorded as an episode within the Chhim leh Hmar Indo (South-North inter-clan war).

Historical accounts (including the Wikipedia entry on Herbert Richard Browne) name Khalkam (also Kalkhama) as the Lushai Sailo chief who broke his oath of fealty and orchestrated the September 1890 ambush that killed Capt. Browne near Changsil — a name that matches none of the four options (Bengkhuaia, Hausata, Zathawma, Ngura). This looks like a genuinely broken question with no correct option; 'Zathawma' is kept only as an unverified closest guess.

The Chin-Lushai Expedition of 1889-90 was commanded by Colonel (Brig.-Gen.) F.V.G. Tregear against the Lushai columns; Generals Brownlow and Bourchier commanded the earlier, separate 1871-72 expedition, a classic distractor here.
N.E. Parry, a British administrator in the Lushai Hills, authored the ethnographic monograph 'The Lakhers' (1932).
Rev. William Williams, the first Christian missionary to Mizoram, departed Silchar on 15 March 1891 and reached Aizawl on 20 March 1891.
Dr. Peter Fraser, a Welsh medical missionary, arrived in 1908 as the first medical missionary in Mizoram and also campaigned against the Bawi (slavery) system.
Around 2,100 Mizos left Aijal to serve in the Indian Labour Corps during the First World War, working in France on fortifications and related labour.
R. Dala was the first editor of Kristian Tlangau, the Welsh Mission's newspaper first published in 1911 and renamed Kristian Tlangau in 1914.
The mautam famine of 1861-1862 is cited as an early, well-documented instance of the recurring bamboo-flowering famine in the Lushai Hills, predating the 1911-12 and 1959 mautam events.

Sources date the launch of the Lushai Hills District Council to 26 April 1952 (by Assam CM Bishnuram Medhi), with its inaugural session running 23 June-10 July 1952 — none of which lines up exactly with any of the four printed options. '25th July, 1952' is kept as the closest available option (matching month and year), but the exact-day discrepancy remains unresolved.
The United Mizo Freedom Organisation (UMFO), formed in 1947 as a split from the Mizo Union, had the objective of uniting Mizo-inhabited areas with kindred tribes in Burma.

The Mizoram Peace Accord (Memorandum of Settlement between the Government of India and the MNF) was signed on 30 June 1986, confirmed by multiple sources including the government's own DIPR account; that exact date is not one of the four options. '25th June, 1986' is the closest option by month and year, but the day is off by five, so this remains unresolved.
The Himalayan Serow (locally 'Saza') is the official state animal of Mizoram.
C. Lalremsanga, an archer who represented India at the 1992 and 1996 Olympics, was conferred the Dhyan Chand Award (lifetime achievement in sports) in 2019.
